Registered Datasets: What an Analyst Needs to Know

John Ehrlinger

2026-10-28

Source: vignettes/registered-datasets.qmd

Open a study’s datasets folder and you will find more files than you expected. Beside built.sas7bdat sit built_20261021.parquet, built_20261021_r2.parquet, a .schema.csv for each, and the same again for every other dataset the study reads. It is natural to wonder which of these your job reads, why the dates in the names do not match the day someone last registered anything, and whether you are supposed to tidy them up.

The short answer is that you never have to look at them. Your job names a dataset, and the package hands it the latest registered version of that dataset. This vignette explains what is underneath, for the day you want to know. It is written for the analyst running jobs. The statistical programmer who builds and registers the data will find the mechanics, and the checksums behind them, in vignette("dataset-versioning").

The worked example

We follow one study through the whole vignette. It reads two datasets, the study dataset built and a second dataset named builtr, each built in SAS. Its datasets folder held, among others, these files on 2026-10-23:

built.sas7bdat                   the SAS file the programmer rebuilds
built_20261021_r2.parquet        the registered version jobs read
built_20261021_r2.schema.csv     its column record
builtr.sas7bdat
builtr_20261021_r3.parquet       the registered version jobs read
builtr_20261021_r3.schema.csv
built_20261007.parquet           earlier versions, kept
built_20261013.parquet
...

and its manifest.yaml recorded the builtr dataset like this, trimmed to the lines that matter here:

- file: builtr.sas7bdat
  parquet: builtr_20261021_r3.parquet
  extract_date: '2026-10-21'
  n_rows: 5955
  n_cols: 176
  source_mtime: 2026-10-21 22:20:03.141081
  history:
  - parquet: builtr_20261021_r2.parquet
  - parquet: builtr_20261021.parquet
  - parquet: builtr_20261016.parquet
  - parquet: builtr_20261015.parquet

Each history entry also carries its own checksums and row and column counts; they are left out above. Every question below is answered from this example.

What Does Registering a Dataset Do?

The SAS file in datasets is a working file. The programmer rebuilds it as often as the build needs, and while they do, nothing you run changes. A job reads data only once it has been registered (accepted as a version of the dataset that jobs may read).

Registering happens once, with register_data(), when a dataset first joins the study. After that the programmer runs one call from anywhere in the study:

hvtiRutilities::update_manifest()

For each dataset whose SAS file has changed since its last registration, that call does three things.

  1. Reads the SAS file and writes it once to a dated parquet file beside it, such as builtr_20261021_r3.parquet. That parquet is the registered version. It is never rewritten afterwards.
  2. Writes the column record beside it, builtr_20261021_r3.schema.csv: each column’s name, type and SAS label.
  3. Records the new version in manifest.yaml: the parquet’s name, its SHA-256 checksum (a fingerprint that changes if a single byte of the file does), the checksum of the SAS file it came from, its date and its row and column counts. The version it replaces moves into the entry’s history.

It prints one line per dataset saying what it did:

builtr: registered builtr_20261021_r3.parquet (5955 rows, 176 columns); previous version kept as builtr_20261021_r2.parquet

A dataset whose SAS file has not changed is reported as unchanged, and no new version is written for it.

Why Is It Named That Way?

A registered version is named <name>_<YYYYMMDD>.parquet, where <name> is the SAS file’s name without its extension. A second version on the same date gets _r2, a third _r3, and so on.

The date is the SAS file’s date, not the day it was registered. Specifically, it is the date the SAS file was last written (its modification date, as a file listing shows it), unless the programmer gave an extract_date when registering. The manifest records no registration date at all.

That explains the two things people notice in the example.

  • builtr_20261021_r3.parquet says 10-21 because builtr.sas7bdat was last written on the evening of 2026-10-21. Had nobody registered it until a week later, the name would still say 10-21, and so would every date the reports give for it.
  • builtr reached _r3 while built stopped at _r2. Each dataset counts its own versions. builtr.sas7bdat was rebuilt and registered three times with a 2026-10-21 date, built.sas7bdat twice.

The _rN suffix therefore says how many times that dataset was registered from a SAS file written on that date. It says nothing about which version is current; the manifest does that.

Which File Does My Job Read?

A job names its dataset at the top, in its study choices:

DATASET <- "builtr"

and reads it by that name. "built" (or leaving the setting at its default) is the study dataset. The package looks the name up in manifest.yaml and reads the version recorded there, after checking its checksum. For the example, that is builtr_20261021_r3.parquet.

So a job that reads a dataset reads its latest registered version, with no file name in your code. When the programmer registers builtr_20261028.parquet next week, your next render reads it, and you change nothing.

Two kinds of job read something else, and say so in their reports.

  • A job that sets ANALYSIS_SET <- "<name>" reads that analysis set, a subset saved from the study dataset by hvtiRdatabuild::write_analysis_set(). Registering a new version of the study dataset makes the set out of date. A draft render still reads the old set, with a note saying so; a final render stops until the set is written again from the new version.
  • A job that reads another job’s saved results, such as an -explain job reading what its -fit job saved, uses the data that job read. Its “About this run” table names that version under Upstream. Re-render the upstream job first to carry new data through.

That is also why nobody needs to open, copy, rename, move or delete a parquet file by hand. Every read checks the checksum of the version it reads, and most jobs run verify_manifest() before they read anything, which checks every registered version, current and earlier. A version that has been moved or edited fails those checks, and the job stops with a message to restore it and tell the study’s data manager. Leave the files where the package puts them.

Which Version Did a Report Use?

Every report rendered from a current job names the version it read in three places. (A job scaffolded before hvtiRtemplates 1.3.1 renders without the box and the “About this run” table.)

  • The box under the title. It reads something like data `builtr` `builtr_20261021_r3.parquet`, dated 2026-10-21. On a working read (HVTI_DATA=working, below) it names the SAS file instead and adds “working read, not a registered version”. A job that sets ANALYSIS_SET names the analysis set instead, with the day the set was written (see below).
  • The data table, captioned “The data this job read”. Its first row, Source, names the dataset and the version file, dataset `builtr` (builtr_20261021_r3.parquet), followed by the rows read and kept.
  • The “About this run” table at the end. Under Dataset `builtr` it lists the version file, its Version date, the source file it came from, the rows and patients kept, the WHERE conditions, the first 12 characters of the version’s SHA-256, and a Manifest row that says current, newer file waiting, or not in the manifest (the file read is no registered version).

For a registered dataset, the dated date in the box and the Version date row give the version’s date, the one in its file name: the SAS file’s date, as above. An analysis set’s written date is something else: the day write_analysis_set() cut the set, which can be weeks after the version it was cut from. A set written today from built_20260915.parquet reads written 2026-10-24, which says nothing about how fresh the data are. The same facts, with the full checksum, are written into the report’s embedded provenance record, so a figure can be traced back to the exact file months later.

Older reports word two of these differently, and their labels tell them apart. Their box says registered 2026-10-21 where a newer one says dated, and their “About this run” table has a Registered row where a newer one has Version date. (Go by the labels, not by the hvtiRtemplates version at the end of the box: the version still read 1.5.0 for a while after the new labels arrived.) That date is the same version date, not the day the version was registered. Their box is also written before the job reads anything, so on a working read it still names the registered version while the Source row and “About this run” name the working SAS file. In such a report, believe the Source row and “About this run”.

What If the SAS File Changes and Nobody Registers It?

Suppose the programmer rebuilds builtr.sas7bdat on 2026-10-24 and does not run update_manifest(). Your job still reads builtr_20261021_r3.parquet. Its results are what they were, because the data it reads have not changed.

The job tells you a newer file is waiting. The data table ends with a Note row. In it, “registered on” gives the version’s date, the SAS file’s date, not the day it was registered:

builtr.sas7bdat has changed since it was registered on 2026-10-21. This job used
the registered version, builtr_20261021_r3.parquet. Review it with
hvtiRutilities::review_built(), then run hvtiRutilities::update_manifest() to
register it.

The Manifest row in “About this run” says newer file waiting, and verify_manifest() lists the SAS file as PENDING. None of these stops the job, and none makes the report a draft. The report is a correct report of the registered version. Whether the rebuild should become the next version is the programmer’s call, and the note is your cue to ask.

A report is marked a draft for other reasons: an EDIT: marker still in the job, a skipped chunk, or a stop_here(). The box under the title then reads draft and counts them. One more case reads the SAS file itself rather than a registered version, a working read:

HVTI_DATA=working quarto render 10_descriptive/table1.qmd

A dataset that has never been registered is read this way too, whether or not you asked. A working read is allowed in the interactive console and in a draft render of a job in any stage folder. It prints “Results from it are a draft”, and you should treat the report that way. A final render (render_job(final = TRUE)), a script run with Rscript, and a job at the study root or outside the study refuse it and stop. The message says to unset HVTI_DATA when a registered version exists, and to register the dataset with update_manifest() when none does.

Where Do the Older Versions Go?

Every registered version is kept, so a manuscript revision can be reproduced from the version its paper used. Older releases of the package keep them all beside the SAS file, which is how the example’s folder filled up.

From the release that carries hvtiRutilities #243, update_manifest() moves the version it replaces, with its .schema.csv and build record, into datasets/_archive/. Only the current version of each dataset sits beside its SAS file, and Quarto skips _archive/ as it skips every folder whose name starts with _.

  • manifest.yaml is unchanged. It still lists every version by name and checksum, and verify_manifest() checks each one, beside the SAS file or in _archive/.
  • A study registered before that release needs nothing done. Its next registration moves every earlier version still beside the SAS file.
  • Two kinds of file stay beside the SAS file: a version file that is a symbolic link, and one that another registered dataset reads as its source. The package still finds them there.
  • _archive/ is the package’s to manage, as the datasets folder is. Do not move files into it or out of it yourself.
  • Verify an archived study with that release or a later one. An older verify_manifest() looks only beside the SAS file and reports the archived versions as missing. Studies pin their hvtiRutilities version through renv, so this matters only if analysts on one study run different versions.

In Short

You want to Do this
Read the data Set DATASET <- "<name>" in the job; it reads the latest registered version
Know which version a report used Read the box under the title, the data table’s Source row, or “About this run”
Know whether newer data exist Look for a Note row in the data table, or newer file waiting in “About this run”
Get newer data into your job Ask the programmer to review and register it with update_manifest(), then re-render
Tidy the datasets folder Nothing; the package manages it
